sm: Ben Shapiro walks through scenes from his film Confession and explains what was happening behind the scenes. In the first scene, the interrogator Vladimir, played by James Franco, presses Rob's character Alexei to sign a confession in exchange for his wife's release, arguing that good and evil are luxuries the revolution cannot afford. Shapiro calls the argument pure Machiavelli: power moves history, and evil means are sometimes needed for a higher good. Alexei answers that embracing evil to reach good only produces evil. Shapiro says the two men define evil differently, one as moral evil and the other as material conditions like poverty and starvation, and that he tried to give each side its strongest case. In the next scene, Richard Brake plays Bogdan, a committed Marxist who correctly accuses Alexei of missing the forest for the artistic trees. Shapiro praises the actors and says the script leaves room for them to make their own choices.

Shapiro describes the opening sequence, in which Alexei is thrown into a standing cell, a real feature of communist prisons, too small to sit or lie down in. This was not in the original script. Director Vojtech Vosloo, who is from Czechoslovakia and knows communist history through his family, asked for it to be added. Shapiro notes that only a couple of minutes of the two hour ten minute film are scored, so lighting, sound design, camera movement and staging carry it. He says Vosloo called it the biggest challenge of his career to make two rooms visually interesting. Shapiro then discusses a scene in which Jennifer Jason Lee's character Anya tells Alexei his sacrifice is meaningless. He told her she is right in this argument, as a mother defending her family against Alexei's idealism. He praises her raw performance and the whole cast, comparing it to a baseball team where every reliever throws a hundred. He hopes viewers ask who is right, what they would do, and what faith is worth.
